newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's Hopewell outlook clouded by Thai project.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Hopewell outlook clouded by Thai project.

text.p: Hopewell Holdings Ltd shares have been on a winning streak this week but analysts said on Thursday they were not optimistic about the infrastructure firm's outlook due mainly to its Bangkok mass transit project.
"Bearish," W.I. Carr analyst Wendy Ko said of its outlook.
"I am not positive towards its Thai project, and it's their major project," she said, referring to the US$3.2 billion, 44 km (27 mile) Bangkok mass transit project.
HSBC James Capel research analyst Leon Chik said the firm's development would be constrained by a lack of constant additions of new projects. "The company's prospects are so far limited," he said.
The stock added HK$0.075 on Tuesday and a further HK$0.225 on Wednesday before closing unchanged at HK$4.725 (US$0.61) on Thursday.
Analysts attributed the gains partly to rumours that Cheung Kong Infrastructure Holdings Ltd (CKI) would take a stake in Hopewell or its projects.
CKI has denied the talk. "We have denied that," said Tony Tsoi, senior manager in planning and investment at CKI.

But Michael Brueukels, utilities analyst at UBS Securities, said CKI may still take a stake in certain Hopewell projects, particularly in China. "A denial should not mean that nothing is forthcoming," he said.

"CKI and Hopewell are already together in the development of the ringroad project around Guangzhou. So it might be that CKI is looking to increase their stake or possibly take a stake in one of the southern China (projects)," Brueukels said.
Any CKI investment in projects of debt-laden Hopewell would be viewed positively, he added.
Analysts also said Hopewell shares were trading at a significant discount to net asset value, which is estimated at between HK$6.70 and HK$7.50.
Despite the recent price gains, analysts said the firm faced a tough future with problems dogging the Bangkok project.
Last week, Thailand said it would fine Hopewell six million baht (US$230,000) per day if the firm failed to complete the initial stage of the project on schedule.
Wrangles between the firm and state agencies have led to serious delays in the project, in which Hopewell said it has already invested between HK$3 billion and HK$4 billion.

The firm was quoted by a Thai official as saying it had proposed increasing the registered capital of its Thai unit responsible for the project to 30 billion baht (US$1.15 billion) by the end of this year from six billion baht (US$230.8 million).

"That's a big injection. That just means they are going to get squeezed again for cash. Basically they need to reduce their debt level but at the same time they need to increase their equity injection in Thailand," Brueukels said.
"I think they have to do that (increase equity) before anybody comes forward and says here's some money we're willing to loan you."
No updated figure on the firm's debt position was available.

But chairman Gordon Wu said last October its gearing would fall from 92 percent to as low as 23 percent after debt repayments with the proceeds from the sale, completed last month, of an 80 percent stake in Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd (CEPA) to U.S. utility Southern Co for HK$10.8 billion.
Ko said she did not expect good returns from the Bangkok project because of high costs and the poor Thai property market.

"The idea of the project is to supplement returns (from roads) with property earnings. But as the Thai property market is so bad...and the project costs are so high, it won't be able to generate a satisfactory return on investement," she said.
